# Microsoft FY26 10-K: Filing Skeleton Only—No Financial Data Extracted

## Executive summary
- The PDF passed to this workflow contains only the EDGAR submission header, a document index listing 130 files, and the text of three insider-trading policy exhibits (EX-19.1, EX-19.2, EX-19.3).
- No consolidated financial statements, Management's Discussion and Analysis, segment footnotes, or earnings press release (8-K Exhibit 99.1) text appears in the extraction.
- Fiscal year end is confirmed as **2026-06-30** (Microsoft uses a June 30 fiscal year); filing acceptance date **2026-07-29**.
- Without the body of the 10-K, revenue, net income (GAAP and non-GAAP), EPS, operating cash flow, dividends, and all other metrics cannot be populated.
- This memo serves as a placeholder; re-extraction of the full HTML filing (msft-20260630.htm, 8.6 MB per the index) is required to deliver the standard buyside analysis.

## Key numbers
**Not applicable.** The text provided does not include Item 8 consolidated financial statements, Item 7 MD&A, or any earnings summary table. The EDGAR index confirms that Document 1 (msft-20260630.htm, Sequence 1, iXBRL format, 8,585,501 bytes) is the substantive 10-K, but its content was not passed to the analyst workflow—only the outer wrapper and three policy exhibits were extracted.

## Non-GAAP framing
**Not applicable.** No reconciliation or non-GAAP table is present in the provided text. Historically Microsoft reports both GAAP and non-GAAP net income and diluted EPS, excluding stock-based compensation, integration/restructuring costs, and certain tax adjustments. Analysis of whether those exclusions remain defensible for FY26 must await access to the full filing.

## Segments
**Not applicable.** Microsoft typically reports three operating segments: Productivity and Business Processes (Office, LinkedIn, Dynamics), Intelligent Cloud (Azure, server products, enterprise services), and More Personal Computing (Windows, Devices, Gaming, Search). No segment revenue, gross margin, or operating income figures are present in the extracted text.

## Quality of earnings
**Not applicable.** Cash-conversion metrics (operating cash flow vs net income, free cash flow, working-capital movements, deferred revenue changes, DSO, inventory turns) cannot be calculated without the consolidated statement of cash flows and balance sheet.

## Balance sheet
**Not applicable.** Cash and short-term investments, total debt, net cash / net debt, shareholders' equity, share count (basic and diluted), and any material changes in deferred revenue or contract liabilities cannot be assessed.

## Guidance and outlook
**Not applicable.** Item 7 MD&A and any forward-looking commentary on FY27 revenue or EPS ranges are absent from the provided text. Microsoft does not typically provide full-year EPS guidance in the 10-K itself (guidance is given quarterly on earnings calls), but directional commentary on cloud Azure growth, AI monetization, and capital-expenditure plans is usually found in MD&A—none of which is available here.

## Capital allocation
**Not applicable.** Dividend per share (Microsoft historically pays a quarterly cash dividend, increased annually in September), share-buyback authorization size, shares actually repurchased during FY26, and remaining authorization capacity cannot be determined. Insider selling disclosures (required in the proxy, not the 10-K) and any commentary on M&A (e.g., pending Activision Blizzard close or new AI-related acquisitions) are also missing.

## Management framing
**Assessment: Not applicable (no MD&A or earnings release text provided).**

The three exhibits that *were* extracted—EX-19.1 (General Insider Trading Policy), EX-19.2 (Restricted Trading Window Policy), and EX-19.3 (Section 16 Officer and Director Preclearance Policy)—are standard governance documents. They confirm that:
- All Microsoft employees may not trade in Microsoft or other company securities while in possession of material, nonpublic information.
- Corporate vice presidents and above, plus other designated insiders, may trade Microsoft stock only during quarterly open windows (beginning the second trading day after earnings release, ending the 10th calendar day of the third month of the fiscal quarter).
- Section 16 officers and directors must preclear all trades, including option exercises and gifts, with CELA Corporate Legal (emails redacted as (**)).
- Insiders are prohibited from trading in derivatives (puts, calls), from pledging Microsoft stock as loan collateral, and from using confidential information in prediction markets or event contracts.
- Any late Section 16 filings are disclosed in the annual proxy statement.

These policies are best-practice and typical for a large-cap issuer; they do not, however, provide any insight into FY26 financial performance.

## Positives
- **Fiscal discipline**: The fact that the 10-K was filed on July 29, 2026—exactly on time for a June 30 year-end—indicates a well-controlled close process.
- **Governance**: The detailed insider-trading policies, including specific language prohibiting prediction-market bets using confidential information (added in recent years to address crypto and event-contract platforms), reflect strong compliance culture.

## Negatives / red flags
- **Incomplete extraction**: This is not a negative about Microsoft; it is a workflow issue. The buyside analyst cannot evaluate revenue growth, margin trajectory, cloud-monetization trends, AI-capex efficiency, or cash-return sustainability without the actual financial statements and MD&A.
- **No earnings press release**: The 8-K with Exhibit 99.1 (the quarterly or annual earnings release that frames non-GAAP results and provides management commentary) is not referenced in the document index provided. Microsoft typically files an 8-K the same day as the 10-K for year-end, or within two business days of each quarterly earnings announcement. That 8-K would contain the summary P&L table, segment revenue, and forward guidance that buyside investors rely on.

## Bottom line
**Bull case (not assessable from this filing skeleton):** Microsoft in prior years has delivered consistent double-digit revenue growth driven by Azure (often 25–35% constant-currency growth), commercial cloud gross margin expansion, and rising operating leverage in Productivity (Office 365, LinkedIn) and Gaming (Xbox, Game Pass, Activision content post-acquisition). If FY26 continued that trajectory, the bull case rests on Azure + AI monetization, stable 40%+ operating margins, and US\$70–80 billion annual free cash flow supporting both dividend growth and US\$15–20 billion quarterly buybacks.

**Bear case (not assessable from this filing skeleton):** The bear worries would be decelerating Azure growth (law of large numbers), rising AI-infrastructure capex (US\$30–40 billion annually) that pressures free-cash-flow conversion, margin compression from lower-margin AI services, regulatory headwinds (EU Digital Markets Act, US antitrust scrutiny of Teams bundling and GitHub/OpenAI vertical integration), and share dilution from continued heavy stock-based compensation (typically US\$8–10 billion per year, material relative to net income).

**What would change the view:** Access to the full 10-K (Item 8 financials, Item 7 MD&A, Item 1A risk factors updated for AI, cybersecurity, and export controls) and the paired FY26 earnings 8-K. Specifically:
1. **Azure revenue and remaining performance obligation (RPO)** to gauge multi-year cloud backlog.
2. **GAAP vs non-GAAP net income reconciliation** to verify that stock-based comp, restructuring, and tax adjustments remain one-off or truly non-recurring.
3. **Operating cash flow and free cash flow** (operating cash less capex) to assess whether AI capex is cannibalizing shareholder distributions.
4. **Segment operating margins**, particularly Intelligent Cloud, to test whether incremental AI revenue is accretive or dilutive.
5. **Share count and buyback detail** to confirm that buybacks are offsetting SBC dilution (historically they do, but the ratio matters).
6. **Forward guidance** on FY27 revenue, operating income, and any commentary on AI product monetization timelines (Copilot pricing and attach rates, OpenAI revenue share).
7. **Debt maturity schedule and cash domicile** (domestic vs foreign) to evaluate refinancing risk and tax-efficient capital return.

Once the full filing text is available, return it to this workflow and the standard forensic equity memo—metrics table, segment deep-dive, cash-quality assessment, management-honesty verdict, and actionable bull/bear—will be generated in accordance with the buyside standard.

---

**Prepared by:** Bob USA (buyside forensic analyst)  
**Source documents:** SEC EDGAR filing 0001193125-26-323660 (cover page and exhibits only; full 10-K HTML not extracted)  
**Fiscal period:** Year ended June 30, 2026  
**Filing date:** July 29, 2026  
**Note:** This memo is a placeholder. Re-run analysis with complete filing text to populate all metrics and deliver actionable investment insight.

- (Note: there is a US$0.7b difference between the C&N segment total US$88.3b and the Data Center platform total US$89.0b; the filing does not reconcile this, likely due to automotive revenue being split between segments or platform reporting overlaps. Graphics is Edge Computing in the market-platform view: GeForce GPUs for gaming and PCs, RTX/Quadro for workstations. Revenue growth was driven by Blackwell workstation GPUs, partially offset by weaker consumer PC sales (elevated memory and system prices dampened consumer demand). Graphics is rounding-error scale versus Data Center.

China: NVIDIA disclosed that Data Center Hopper product shipments to China in Q2 FY27 were less than 1% of Data Center revenue (under US$890m). The US government granted licenses to ship small quantities of H200 to specific China-based customers starting in February 2026, but the PRC government restricted those sales, and NVIDIA has been unable to sell all the licensed products. Earlier, in August 2025, the USG granted licenses for certain H20 products to China, but the PRC government again restricted sales, and NVIDIA sold no H20 inventory. As a result, NVIDIA incurred a US$4.5b charge in Q1 FY26 for H20 excess inventory and purchase obligations, and a further US$0.4b charge in Q1 FY27 for H200. China data center revenue is effectively zero; competitors (Chinese GPU makers, AMD, others) are gaining share in that market.

**Cash conversion:** Operating cash flow for 1H FY27 was US$74.4b, covering 63% of the US$118.0b net income for the same period. The gap is explained by working capital, primarily receivables. Accounts receivable rose US$24.6b sequentially from Jan 25 to Jul 26, 2026. Management states this is due to extended payment terms (90 days to one year) on large multi-quarter agreements with certain investment-grade customers who are building data centers. These arrangements help customers manage large-scale infrastructure capex but delay NVIDIA's cash collection. DSO is not disclosed but is clearly elevated.

Inventories rose US$10.2b in 1H FY27, reflecting the buildup of components (memory, advanced packaging) and work-in-process for the Blackwell and Rubin ramp. Management increased supply commitments from US$119b last quarter to US$279b as of Jul 26, 2026 (disclosed in Note 10) to secure future capacity; if demand or mix shifts, this creates write-down risk.

**Provisions and one-offs:** Inventory provisions and excess purchase-obligation charges totaled US$985m in Q2 FY27 and US$2.1b in 1H FY27. Provision releases from sales of previously reserved inventory and settlements were US$177m in Q2 and US$280m in 1H, for a net unfavorable impact on gross margin of 0.8% and 1.0% respectively. For comparison, in Q2 FY26 the net impact was -1.1%, and in 1H FY26 it was -5.9% (driven by the US$4.5b H20 charge in Q1 FY26). Excluding the H20/H200 charges, the provision activity is routine and modest relative to the scale of the business.

**Stock-based compensation:** SBC was US$4.0b in 1H FY27, or 2.2% of revenue. R&D expense (excluding SBC) was approximately US$9.4b for the half (US$13.4b total R&D less ~US$3.0b SBC embedded in R&D per the footnote breakdown on page 12). SBC is material but not egregious; it is a real cost and appropriately expensed. As a percentage of revenue, SBC has fallen due to revenue scale.

**Accounts receivable quality:** The US$24.6b receivables increase is large but management attributes it to extended terms for investment-grade customers. The filing does not disclose customer credit ratings or specific counterparties. Given NVIDIA's customer concentration (one direct customer 16% of Q2 revenue; three direct customers 16%, 15%, 13% of 1H revenue, all C&N segment), the working capital swing is lumpy. There is no disclosure of overdue balances or allowance changes. Receivables are a timing issue, not a bad-debt issue, but the cash lag is real.

## Balance sheet

**Cash and liquidity:** Cash and equivalents US$22.4b, marketable debt securities US$34.1b, total US$56.6b. Up US$6.9b from Jan 25, 2026 despite returning US$46.1b to shareholders (US$39.8b buybacks, US$6.3b dividends) in the first half. The company issued US$25.0b of long-term debt in June 2026 (seven tranches, maturities from 2028 to 2056, weighted effective rate approximately 4.7%) for general corporate purposes. That debt issuance funded the buybacks and left net cash relatively flat despite the operating cash flow shortfall versus net income.

**Debt:** Total debt principal US$33.5b (up from US$8.5b at Jan 25, 2026). Includes the new US$25b June 2026 issuance plus existing notes (US$1.0b due 2026, US$1.25b due 2028, US$1.25b due 2031, US$1.0b due 2040, US$2.0b due 2050, US$0.5b due 2060). Net debt (gross debt less cash + marketable debt) is US$-23.1b, i.e. net cash of US$23.1b excluding the US$42.8b of marketable equity securities. Including the equity portfolio (which is volatile and subject to lock-up restrictions totaling US$36.9b as of Jul 26), total net cash is US$66b. The company has a US$25b commercial paper program with zero drawn.

**Equity securities:** Marketable equity securities US$42.8b, up from US$12.9b at Jan 25, 2026. These are publicly-held shares and warrants (Level 1 US$37.0b, Level 2 unregistered warrants and convertible preferreds US$10.8b). The filing states US$36.9b is subject to short-term lock-up restrictions (sale restrictions); US$5.0b of the Level 1 holdings is subject to lock-up through December 2027 and is classified in "Other assets" on the balance sheet. Unrealized gains on these positions in Q2 FY27 were US$1.5b; for 1H FY27, US$12.5b. The company also holds US$47.9b of non-marketable equity securities (private companies, valued at cost less impairment plus observable price changes). Total equity investment exposure is thus US$90.7b. Of this, Note 6 states NVIDIA has equity investment commitments of US$25b and recorded US$99b of equity investments on the balance sheet (the difference is likely timing of Note 6 disclosure versus the rollforward table, or may include loans / other instruments). This is a massive equity portfolio concentrated in AI infrastructure, AI model makers, and ecosystem companies. If those valuations correct, it will flow through "Other income, net" and could swing quarterly results by billions.

**Deferred revenue:** US$6.4b (current US$4.6b, long-term US$1.8b), up from US$2.6b at Jan 25. Includes US$2.8b of customer advances as of Jul 26, suggesting customers are pre-paying for future Blackwell / Rubin shipments. The filing states US$3.2b of future revenue from contracts >1 year in length is deferred or unbilled, of which 39% will be recognized over the next 12 months. This is routine for large systems contracts.

**Share count:** Diluted shares outstanding 24.3b in Q2 FY27, down from 24.5b in Q2 FY26. NVIDIA repurchased 203m shares for US$39.8b in 1H FY27, reducing the share count by 0.8% year-over-year despite the addition of ~100m dilutive shares from equity awards. The company has US$99.3b of remaining buyback authorization as of Jul 26, 2026. Share count is declining modestly despite heavy SBC issuance.

## Guidance and outlook

NVIDIA does NOT provide formal revenue or EPS guidance in this 10-Q. The MD&A says the company is experiencing supply constraints for Blackwell and Rubin (both shipping concurrently) and that demand estimates can be inaccurate, creating revenue or supply volatility. Management states they are working to secure inventory and capacity for the next several years and have increased supply commitments from US$119b last quarter to US$279b. The commitments table (Note 10) is a forward-looking proxy for growth expectations: US$120b in the remainder of FY27 (2H FY27), US$100b in FY28, US$98b in FY29, then tapering. The trajectory implies sustained high revenue but also a plateau in the out-years.

No earnings-per-share or margin guide was given. Management noted gross margin was "approximately flat sequentially as our Blackwell architecture remains the vast majority of our revenue," suggesting mix is stable near current levels (75%). The absence of explicit forward guidance is notable -- it allows maximum flexibility on supply and mix but offers no anchor for investors modeling FY27 or FY28.

## Capital allocation

Dividends: On May 18, 2026, the board increased the quarterly cash dividend from US$0.01 to US$0.25 per share, a 25-fold increase. Q2 FY27 dividend declared and paid was US$0.25 × ~24.2b shares = US$6.0b cash. For the first half, total dividends paid were US$6.3b. The new run rate is ~US$25b per year. At the current share price (not disclosed in the filing, but the filing is dated Aug 26, 2026 and average prices can be inferred from the buyback table), the yield is immaterial (~0.4% annualized if shares trade around US$200). The 25× increase signals confidence, not income orientation.

Buybacks: US$19.7b in Q2 FY27 (94m shares at an average price of ~US$209), US$39.8b in 1H FY27 (203m shares). The board authorized an additional US$80b on May 18, 2026; total remaining authorization is US$99.3b. Buybacks were executed via open market, Rule 10b5-1 plans, and structured repurchase agreements. The company incurred a 1% excise tax on net repurchases (Inflation Reduction Act 2022), which was not broken out separately but is embedded in the cost of repurchases. Buyback pace is aggressive: annualizing 1H implies ~US$80b per year, which would exhaust the authorization in under 15 months unless extended again.

Combined return in 1H FY27: US$46.1b (dividends + buybacks), funded by US$74.4b operating cash flow less US$4.4b capex and the US$25b debt issuance. Without the debt issuance, free cash flow would have been insufficient to cover the capital return, hence the bond market access.

## Management framing: Mixed

The MD&A is factual and detailed. Management disclosed the China export-control losses (US$4.9b cumulative charges), the working capital increase from extended payment terms, and the supply constraints for Blackwell and Rubin. The tone is sober: "Demand estimates for our products can be inaccurate and create volatility in our revenue or supply levels" and "we are currently experiencing certain supply constraints." The filing does not spin the China situation; it states plainly that NVIDIA is "effectively foreclosed from competing in China's data center computing/compute market" and that the loss of opportunity and the benefit to competitors will have a "material and adverse impact on our business, operating results, and financial condition."

However, the company did NOT provide formal guidance, which limits accountability and makes it harder to assess execution next quarter. The decision to ramp Blackwell and Rubin simultaneously is described as a response to demand, but it also introduces complexity and potential for margin or yield issues that are not quantified.

On capital allocation, the US$80b buyback authorization and the 25× dividend increase are presented as shareholder-friendly but occurred in the same quarter the company issued US$25b of debt, suggesting the cash flow (despite being US$74b in 1H) is not sufficient to fund both growth capex and the new return policy. The company is levering the balance sheet to return capital while the stock trades near all-time highs; that is defensible if the growth continues but increases risk if the cycle turns.

Overall framing: Transparent on the bad news (China, working capital, supply risk), silent on forward guidance, and promotional on capital return. Mixed.

## Positives

- Revenue growth of 106% year-over-year and 18% sequentially is exceptional; NVIDIA is capturing the AI infrastructure buildout.
- Gross margin of 75% is among the highest in semiconductors and improved 260 bps year-over-year despite the scale of shipments, indicating sustained pricing power.
- Operating cash flow of US$74.4b in the first half is massive in absolute terms, even if it lagged net income growth due to working capital timing.
- The company returned US$46.1b to shareholders in six months (US$39.8b buybacks, US$6.3b dividends) and raised the quarterly dividend 25×, signaling confidence.
- Blackwell and Rubin are both shipping, giving NVIDIA a two-generation product overlap that competitors (AMD, Intel) do not have; this sustains the technology lead.
- The US$279b of supply commitments locks in capacity for several years, reducing the risk of a supply shortfall if demand continues.
- Non-GAAP adjustments are absent (no formal non-GAAP EPS), meaning the reported GAAP results are the actual results; SBC is expensed appropriately.

## Negatives / red flags

- NVIDIA is shut out of China's data center compute market (less than 1% of Data Center revenue) and has written off US$4.9b in the past year for unsellable H20 and H200 inventory and purchase obligations; competitors are entrenched and NVIDIA's return to China is unlikely under current US and PRC policies.
- Operating cash flow of US$74.4b covered only 63% of net income (US$118.0b) in 1H FY27 due to a US$24.6b increase in receivables from extended payment terms; this is a timing mismatch, but it means NVIDIA is financing customers and the cash conversion lag could persist for quarters.
- The company issued US$25b of debt in June 2026 despite having US$56.6b of cash and marketable debt securities, because it needed the proceeds to fund US$46.1b of capital return (dividends + buybacks); free cash flow alone was insufficient. This is financial engineering -- levering the balance sheet to return capital while shares trade at elevated multiples.
- Inventory rose US$10.2b in the half and supply commitments jumped from US$119b to US$279b; if demand or product mix shifts (e.g. customers delay Rubin purchases to wait for the next architecture, or a competitor closes the performance gap), NVIDIA will face large write-downs.
- Total equity investment exposure (marketable + non-marketable) is US$90.7b, much of it in early-stage AI companies and AI infrastructure financiers. These are marked to market (for public holdings) or fair-valued quarterly (for private holdings). If the AI investment cycle corrects, NVIDIA will record billions in losses through "Other income, net," creating quarterly earnings volatility unrelated to the core business.
- Gross margin of 75% is at risk from yield issues or competitive pressure. The filing states margin was "approximately flat sequentially as our Blackwell architecture remains the vast majority of our revenue," but the simultaneous Blackwell + Rubin ramp introduces manufacturing complexity (dual supply chains, dual test/packaging flows). Any yield or cost issue will be magnified by the scale of shipments.
- The filing added new risk-factor disclosures on: (i) commitments, guarantees and commercial arrangements (US$108.5b of total guarantees including the US$105b SB Energy / OpenAI PORTS Technology Campus guarantee signed in August 2026, capped but still a massive contingent liability); (ii) AI cloud agreements where NVIDIA commits to cloud capacity that the provider can unilaterally stop providing to NVIDIA and sell to third parties (US$36b of commitments as of Jul 26); (iii) financing arrangements and extended payment terms that affect operating cash flow timing. All three are new, large, and complex; execution risk is high.
- Management did not provide formal guidance for revenue or EPS, making it impossible to hold them accountable to a forecast next quarter; the omission is a negative signal.
- The China regulatory inquiry disclosed on page 19 states that on September 15, 2025, China's antitrust regulators published a preliminary finding that NVIDIA's compliance with US export controls (offering degraded products to the China market) discriminated unfairly against Chinese customers and violated the terms of the Mellanox acquisition approval. If regulators conclude NVIDIA violated Chinese law, the company could face financial penalties, restrictions on its networking business, or other orders. The risk is open-ended and unquantifiable.

## Bottom line

**Bull case:** NVIDIA is the sole supplier of the AI compute infrastructure that every hyperscaler, AI cloud, and enterprise is building. Blackwell and Rubin are both shipping, and the US$279b of locked-in supply commitments (nearly 3× the annual revenue run rate) guarantee the company can meet demand for the next several years. Gross margin of 75% is structurally defensible because no competitor (AMD, Intel, Chinese GPU makers) has the full-stack integration of hardware, software (CUDA, NIM, etc.) and ecosystem. The US$46b returned to shareholders in 1H FY27 is a rounding error relative to the US$229b of equity and the US$118b of net income; the company can afford to lever the balance sheet and still compound at high rates. The China loss is a sunk cost; the rest of the world is growing fast enough to offset it. If the AI infrastructure buildout continues for another 2-3 years, NVIDIA will compound earnings at 50%+ and the current valuation (not disclosed here but implied by the market cap vs the run rate) is reasonable.

**Bear case:** NVIDIA's revenue is 92% Data Center, and Data Center revenue is concentrated among a handful of hyperscalers and AI clouds whose capex plans can change quarter to quarter. The US$24.6b receivables increase and the US$36b of AI cloud agreements where the provider can unilaterally stop providing capacity to NVIDIA both signal that NVIDIA is financing and de-risking its customers' buildouts, not the other way around. The US$90.7b equity portfolio is a venture capital book masquerading as semiconductor earnings; if AI startups and infrastructure financiers cannot monetize the compute they are buying, that portfolio will implode and take billions out of "Other income" each quarter. The US$279b of supply commitments lock NVIDIA into buying components and capacity at today's prices; if the cycle turns, those become write-offs. The US$105b PORTS guarantee for OpenAI's Ohio data center is a bet-the-company contingent liability dressed up as an ecosystem partnership. The simultaneous Blackwell and Rubin ramp is a manufacturing stretch that will pressure yields and margins. The stock is priced for perfection; any demand slowdown, any yield issue, any margin miss will cause a re-rating. China is lost, and France/EU may be next if regulators decide to restrict NVIDIA on competition grounds. The absence of guidance is management buying optionality to lower the bar.

**What would change my view:**
- (Bull) Management reinstates formal quarterly guidance and beats it for three consecutive quarters; gross margin holds above 74% even as Rubin scales; operating cash flow converges back to net income within two quarters (receivables stop growing, implying customers are paying on schedule); equity portfolio mark-to-market swings are <5% of quarterly net income. If all four occur, the growth story is real and sustainable.
- (Bear) Q3 or Q4 FY27 revenue growth decelerates to +10% q/q or less (implying demand saturation); gross margin falls below 72% (yield or competitive pressure); operating cash flow is <75% of net income for a second consecutive quarter (working capital deteriorates further); or the company takes a >US$5b equity portfolio impairment (AI bubble pops). Any one of these four is a red flag; two or more and the thesis is broken.

Current assessment: The metrics are extraordinary (106% revenue growth, 75% gross margin, US$74b operating cash flow in a half). The risks are also extraordinary (US$108.5b of guarantees, US$90.7b equity portfolio, China locked out, no guidance, cash conversion lag). At this scale and this valuation, there is no room for error. The next two quarters will show whether the supply commitments and customer financing arrangements are bridging a temporary mismatch or papering over a demand peak. Hold if you own it, but watch the working capital and the gross margin like a hawk. If receivables are still climbing in Q3 FY27 or gross margin dips below 74%, sell."

## Executive summary
- Revenue +10% reported (8% constant currency) to US$5,653m; Sleep & Breathing Health US$4,978m (+10%), Residential Care Software US$676m (+5%).
- Non-GAAP gross margin expanded 240 bps to 62.4%, non-GAAP operating margin up 180 bps to 36.1%; GAAP figures depressed by US$42m Astral field-safety notification charge and US$22m restructuring.
- Non-GAAP net income US$1,632m (+16%), non-GAAP diluted EPS US$11.17 (+17%); GAAP net income US$1,523m (+9%), GAAP EPS US$10.43 (+10%).
- Operating cash flow US$1,806m (+3%), free cash flow US$1,650m (-1%); capex US$156m. Cash conversion ratio (OCF/net income) fell to 119% from 125% prior year.
- MatrixCare sale announced June 30, 2026 for US$490m; VirtuOx (IDTF) and Noctrix (RLS device) acquired in FY25/26, adding diagnostic and adjacent-sleep exposure but also HIPAA covered-entity compliance burden and potential Medicare audit risk.

## Key numbers
| Metric | FY26 | FY25 | Change |
|--------|------|------|--------|
| Revenue | US$5,653m | US$5,146m | +10% |
| Gross margin (GAAP) | 61.1% | 59.4% | +170 bps |
| Gross margin (non-GAAP) | 62.4% | 60.0% | +240 bps |
| Operating margin (GAAP) | 33.4% | 32.7% | +70 bps |
| Operating margin (non-GAAP) | 36.1% | 34.3% | +180 bps |
| Net income (GAAP) | US$1,523m | US$1,401m | +9% |
| Net income (non-GAAP) | US$1,632m | US$1,407m | +16% |
| Diluted EPS (GAAP) | US$10.43 | US$9.51 | +10% |
| Diluted EPS (non-GAAP) | US$11.17 | US$9.55 | +17% |
| Operating cash flow | US$1,806m | US$1,752m | +3% |
| Free cash flow | US$1,650m | US$1,662m | -1% |
| Cash + investments | US$1,469m | US$1,209m | +21% |
| Total debt | US$659m | US$668m | -1% |
| Net cash | US$810m | US$541m | +50% |
| Shares outstanding (diluted) | 146.0m | 147.3m | -0.9% |

## Non-GAAP framing
ResMed excluded US$109m (pre-tax) from GAAP to reach non-GAAP net income: amortization of acquired intangibles US$77m (cost-of-sales US$32m, opex US$45m), Astral field-safety notification US$42m, restructuring US$22m, acquisition/portfolio-review costs US$11m, gain on previously held equity investment -US$4m, plus US$39m net tax effect. The adjustments are defensible—amortization of acquisition intangibles is a non-cash charge that does not reflect core operations, the Astral charge is a one-off product quality event, and restructuring is episodic. Stock-based compensation (US$104m, +14% YoY) is treated as a real expense in both GAAP and non-GAAP, which is appropriate; SBC as percentage of revenue rose to 1.8% from 1.8% (flat), and R&D was US$378m, so SBC is 28% of R&D—material but not egregious for a med-tech/software hybrid. The non-GAAP presentation is transparent and within industry norms.

## Segments
**Sleep & Breathing Health (88% of revenue):** US$4,978m, +10% reported (+9% constant currency). Devices US$2,892m (+9% / +7% CC), masks & other US$2,085m (+13% / +12% CC). Americas US$3,281m (+9%): devices +7%, masks +13%. Rest of World US$1,697m (+13% / +7% CC): devices +11% / +6% CC, masks +15% / +9% CC. Mask growth outpaced devices globally, reflecting consumable attach and new-product traction (AirFit/AirTouch portfolio). Margin data not disclosed by sub-segment, but consolidated non-GAAP gross margin for the group rose 240 bps, implying device/mask mix shift and manufacturing productivity gains (Singapore/Sydney production scale, Malaysia ramp) more than offset input-cost inflation and tariff headwinds.

**Residential Care Software (12% of revenue):** US$676m, +5% reported (+4% CC). Brightree (U.S. HME/DME), MEDIFOX DAN (Germany home/nursing), and MatrixCare (U.S. senior living/skilled nursing/home health). Growth decelerated vs Sleep & Breathing; MatrixCare now held-for-sale (close expected Q1 FY27 for US$490m cash), which will reduce this segment by ~40% of revenue (MatrixCare ~US$270m estimated annual revenue based on historical contribution). Post-divestiture, software will be ~7-8% of group revenue. Management cited portfolio optimization to focus on sleep/breathing/connected home health. MEDIFOX DAN and Brightree remain; both are cloud SaaS with recurring revenue, but disclosure of ARR, churn, or net-dollar retention is absent—opacity is a negative for software investors.

## Quality of earnings
GAAP net income US$1,523m converted to operating cash flow US$1,806m (119% conversion), down from 125% in FY25 (US$1,401m net income, US$1,752m OCF). Working capital was a net use: receivables +US$97m (DSO rising as revenue grew faster than collections, potentially reflecting slower HME/DME payor cycles or VirtuOx/Noctrix integration), inventories +US$10m (essentially flat despite 10% revenue growth, indicating improved turns or destocking), payables/accruals +US$173m (benefiting OCF timing). Depreciation & amortization US$201m, SBC US$104m. Capex US$156m (+74% YoY from US$90m) for manufacturing expansion (Calabasas, California greenfield referenced in properties section, Malaysia/Singapore capacity). Free cash flow US$1,650m was -1% YoY despite 16% non-GAAP net-income growth, a disconnect driven by capex step-up and working-capital absorption. No large one-off tax refunds or litigation settlements visible. Quality is good but cash generation lagged profit growth.

## Balance sheet
Cash & equivalents US$1,469m, up US$260m YoY. Total debt US$659m (short-term US$260m, long-term US$399m), down US$9m. Net cash US$810m vs US$541m prior year. Goodwill & intangibles US$3,362m, down US$149m (amortization US$77m, FX -US$40m, MatrixCare reclassified to held-for-sale US$457m asset / US$41m liability). Share count (diluted) 146.0m vs 147.3m, a -0.9% reduction; buybacks totaled US$700m (4.8% of market cap at average price ~US$243), more than offsetting 2.9m shares issued under employee plans (net dilution +0.4m shares after tax withholding). Treasury stock increased US$705m to US$2,779m. Leverage is minimal (net debt/EBITDA ~-0.4x), providing ample capacity for M&A, buybacks, or tariff/supply-chain buffering.

## Guidance and outlook
No explicit FY27 revenue or EPS guide provided. Management stated intention to return >US$1.85bn to shareholders in FY27 via dividends and buybacks, up >85% from FY26's US$1.0bn. Quarterly dividend raised 10% to US$0.66 (US$2.64 annualized), implying ~US$380m annual dividend outlay on current share count; remainder (~US$1.47bn) would be buybacks, or ~10% of market cap at current price. MatrixCare proceeds (US$490m) will fund part of this. Commentary flagged: (i) Philips' U.S. consent decree continues (no firm re-entry timeline), sustaining competitive tailwind; (ii) tariff/supply-chain volatility (Singapore/Malaysia manufacturing mitigates some risk, but magnet/semiconductor sourcing cited as watch item); (iii) VirtuOx (IDTF) and Noctrix (DME) integration—both are direct-bill Medicare entities subject to heightened audit risk and HIPAA covered-entity rules, a new compliance surface for ResMed. FX assumed neutral. Absence of numeric guidance reflects macro uncertainty (GLP-1 obesity-drug impact on OSA severity, U.S. Medicare reimbursement risk under budget reconciliation) but >US$1.85bn capital return is a strong signal of confidence.

## Capital allocation
Dividends US$350m (US$2.40/share annualized at midpoint of FY26), buybacks US$700m; total US$1.05bn returned, vs US$611m in FY25 (+72%). Buyback authorization US$1.0bn remaining at year-end. MatrixCare sale (US$490m) announced June 30, 2026, expected to close Q1 FY27; proceeds earmarked for shareholder returns and/or tuck-in M&A. VirtuOx (FY25, undisclosed consideration) and Noctrix (June 2026, US$325m net of cash) acquisitions broaden the funnel (diagnostic, RLS) but add regulatory/reimbursement execution risk. Capex US$156m (2.8% of revenue) vs US$90m prior year, stepping up for Calabasas and Asia capacity; expect US$180-200m run rate in FY27. No insider-selling data disclosed in 10-K; proxy will be filed within 120 days.

## Management framing: Mixed
The 8-K earnings release and 10-K tone are confident—"strong momentum," "disciplined execution," "market leadership"—but the MatrixCare divestiture signals portfolio course-correction after years of software M&A (Brightree 2016, MatrixCare 2018, HEALTHCAREfirst 2021, MEDIFOX DAN 2022). CEO Mick Farrell's quote emphasizes "focus on core growth areas of sleep, breathing and connected home-based healthcare," implying MatrixCare (senior living/skilled nursing) was a strategic misfit. Positives: transparent non-GAAP reconciliation, clear articulation of Astral/restructuring charges, and >US$1.85bn FY27 capital-return commitment. Negatives: no segment-level margin disclosure, no software ARR/churn metrics, and limited quantification of Philips re-entry risk or GLP-1 demand impact. The Astral field-safety charge (US$42m) was front-footed in cost-of-sales, not buried, which is honest. Risk-factor section expanded to 51 pages (vs ~45 prior year), flagging VirtuOx/Noctrix HIPAA/Medicare compliance, tariff volatility, GLP-1 drugs, and AI regulation—appropriate conservatism. Overall: management is candid about trade-offs but selective in granularity.

## Positives
- Device revenue +9% globally despite Philips still sidelined; mask consumables +13% demonstrate installed-base monetization and new-product (AirSense 11, AirFit portfolio) traction.
- Non-GAAP gross margin 62.4% (+240 bps) and operating margin 36.1% (+180 bps) show scale leverage and manufacturing productivity, even after absorbing US$42m Astral charge in GAAP figures.
- Americas devices +7%, masks +13%; Rest of World devices +11% reported (+6% CC), masks +15% (+9% CC)—broad-based geographic growth.
- Free cash flow US$1,650m (29% of revenue) funds >US$1.85bn FY27 capital return without leveraging the balance sheet (net cash US$810m).
- MatrixCare sale (US$490m) sharpens portfolio; VirtuOx/Noctrix add diagnostic and RLS exposure, expanding TAM beyond OSA.
- Dividend +10% to US$0.66/quarter signals confidence; 5-year CAGR of dividend per share ~8%.
- Cloud-connected devices >35m (myAir >12m registered users) create data moat and switching cost; Smart Comfort FDA-cleared AI feature (launched early 2026) is first mover in personalized CPAP settings.
- Inventory flat YoY despite 10% revenue growth implies improved supply-chain management and turn velocity.

## Negatives / red flags
- Cash conversion deteriorated: OCF +3% vs net income +9%; receivables +US$97m suggests lengthening HME/DME collection cycles or VirtuOx/Noctrix integration friction.
- Capex doubled to US$156m; FY27 likely US$180-200m for Calabasas/Asia expansion—necessary but a near-term FCF drag.
- MatrixCare divestiture (US$490m) at <2x revenue (estimated US$270m annual) implies limited buyer appetite for senior-living software; ResMed's 2018 acquisition cost not disclosed, but likely a write-down embedded in goodwill.
- VirtuOx (IDTF) operates under a 5-year Corporate Integrity Agreement (CIA expires 2027) following US$3m False Claims Act settlement in 2022; any breach triggers exclusion from Medicare. Noctrix (DME) has no national/local Medicare coverage determination, so reimbursement is case-by-case—revenue ramp is uncertain.
- Philips consent decree end-date unknown; if Philips floods U.S. market in FY27, ResMed's device pricing and share could compress. Management cited "competitive dynamics" as a risk but provided no scenario analysis.
- GLP-1 obesity drugs (semaglutide, tirzepatide) now approved for OSA in obese patients; sustained weight loss could reduce OSA severity and long-term device demand. Management acknowledged the risk (10-K page 29) but argued sleep apnea is multifactorial (not obesity alone)—plausible but unquantified.
- Share count reduction -0.9% (1.3m shares) vs US$700m buyback implies average price ~US$538/share equivalent basis—arithmetic suggests buyback at premium to period-average, or SBC dilution higher than net share reduction implies.
- No segment operating-margin disclosure; Residential Care Software (12% of revenue) likely <20% EBIT margin (SaaS norm 25-30%, but MatrixCare/Brightree serve fragmented, price-sensitive SMB customers). Sleep & Breathing likely ~38-40% EBIT margin (devices/masks are 88% of revenue at 62% gross margin), so software is a drag.
- Tariff risk: 10-K cites "new or increased tariffs, reciprocal tariffs, or other disruptions to global trade could have material impact." Singapore/Malaysia production mitigates some U.S.-China exposure, but magnet supply (China controls rare earths) and semiconductor sourcing are vulnerabilities. No quantification of tariff P&L impact provided.
- Restructuring US$22m in FY26 (first restructuring charge in recent history); management cited "realignment of strategies and cost reduction" but gave no detail on headcount cuts or facility closures. Opaque.

## Bottom line
**Bull case:** ResMed is the global leader in sleep apnea with 35m+ cloud-connected devices, a consumables annuity (masks), and a widening moat via AI (Smart Comfort) and data (myAir). Philips' prolonged absence has gifted 18+ months of share gains; even partial Philips return leaves ResMed structurally stronger. Gross margin expansion (240 bps) and 36% non-GAAP operating margin demonstrate operating leverage. MatrixCare exit sharpens focus; VirtuOx/Noctrix extend the franchise into diagnostics and adjacent sleep conditions (RLS). GLP-1 risk is real but overstated—OSA prevalence is rising globally (aging, urbanization, awareness), and weight-loss drugs require sustained adherence (cost, side effects). US$1.85bn+ FY27 capital return (11% of market cap) at 62% gross margin and net-cash balance sheet is investor-friendly. Target US$280-300 (25-27x FY27E P/E of US$11.50-12.00) if Philips re-entry is orderly and tariffs remain contained.

**Bear case:** Philips consent decree lifted in FY27, flooding U.S. market with discounted devices and compressing ResMed's price/mix. GLP-1 drugs gain OSA indication and payer coverage, reducing device starts by 5-10% annually as obesity declines. VirtuOx CIA breach or Noctrix reimbursement denial triggers Medicare audit/clawback and management distraction. Tariffs on Chinese magnets/semiconductors add 200-300 bps to COGS, eroding gross margin to 59-60%. MatrixCare sale at <2x revenue (<US$500m) signals weaker software portfolio than management claimed; Brightree/MEDIFOX churn accelerates as HME/nursing providers adopt vertical-integrated EHRs. Operating cash conversion stays weak (120% vs 130%+ historical) as HME/DME payor cycles lengthen. Multiple compression to 18-20x (medtech norm) implies US$207-230 fair value.

**What would change the view:** (1) Philips U.S. re-entry timeline and pricing—if aggressive (>20% price cut), ResMed's device revenue growth decelerates to mid-single-digit; if delayed beyond FY27, bull case extends. (2) Medicare reimbursement changes—CMS could tighten CPAP coverage criteria (post-AHRQ 2022 study questioning long-term outcomes) or cut payment rates under budget reconciliation; 5-10% rate cut would pressure HME margins and ResMed pricing. (3) GLP-1 real-world OSA remission data—if 30%+ of obese OSA patients achieve durable remission (AHI <5) on GLP-1s, device TAM shrinks materially. (4) VirtuOx/Noctrix integration—if VirtuOx CIA is breached or Noctrix fails to gain coverage, write-down risk and strategic credibility hit. (5) Tariff clarity—if U.S.-China rare-earth/semiconductor tariffs settle at 10-15% and ResMed passes through, neutral; if 25%+ and price absorption required, margin risk. (6) Software ARR disclosure—if ResMed starts reporting Brightree/MEDIFOX ARR and net-dollar retention post-MatrixCare sale, transparency improves and software multiple re-rates upward.

**Accounts receivable quality:** The US$24.6b receivables increase is large but management attributes it to extended terms for investment-grade customers. ## Guidance and outlook

NVIDIA does NOT provide formal revenue or EPS guidance in this 10-Q. The MD&A says the company is experiencing supply constraints for Blackwell and Rubin (both shipping concurrently) and that demand estimates can be inaccurate, creating revenue or supply volatility. Management states they are working to secure inventory and capacity for the next several years and have increased supply commitments from US$119b last quarter to US$279b. The commitments table (Note 10) is a forward-looking proxy for growth expectations: US$120b in the remainder of FY27 (2H FY27), US$100b in FY28, US$98b in FY29, then tapering. The trajectory implies sustained high revenue but also a plateau in the out-years.

No earnings-per-share or margin guide was given. Management noted gross margin was "approximately flat sequentially as our Blackwell architecture remains the vast majority of our revenue," suggesting mix is stable near current levels (75%). The absence of explicit forward guidance is notable -- it allows maximum flexibility on supply and mix but offers no anchor for investors modeling FY27 or FY28.

Dividends: On May 18, 2026, the board increased the quarterly cash dividend from US$0.01 to US$0.25 per share, a 25-fold increase. Q2 FY27 dividend declared and paid was US$0.25 × ~24.2b shares = US$6.0b cash. For the first half, total dividends paid were US$6.3b. The new run rate is ~US$25b per year. At the current share price (not disclosed in the filing, but the filing is dated Aug 26, 2026 and average prices can be inferred from the buyback table), the yield is immaterial (~0.4% annualized if shares trade around US$200). The 25× increase signals confidence, not income orientation.

Buybacks: US$19.7b in Q2 FY27 (94m shares at an average price of ~US$209), US$39.8b in 1H FY27 (203m shares). The board authorized an additional US$80b on May 18, 2026; total remaining authorization is US$99.3b. Buybacks were executed via open market, Rule 10b5-1 plans, and structured repurchase agreements. The company incurred a 1% excise tax on net repurchases (Inflation Reduction Act 2022), which was not broken out separately but is embedded in the cost of repurchases. Buyback pace is aggressive: annualizing 1H implies ~US$80b per year, which would exhaust the authorization in under 15 months unless extended again.

Combined return in 1H FY27: US$46.1b (dividends + buybacks), funded by US$74.4b operating cash flow less US$4.4b capex and the US$25b debt issuance. Without the debt issuance, free cash flow would have been insufficient to cover the capital return, hence the bond market access.

## Management framing: Mixed

The MD&A is factual and detailed. Management disclosed the China export-control losses (US$4.9b cumulative charges), the working capital increase from extended payment terms, and the supply constraints for Blackwell and Rubin. The tone is sober: "Demand estimates for our products can be inaccurate and create volatility in our revenue or supply levels" and "we are currently experiencing certain supply constraints." The filing does not spin the China situation; it states plainly that NVIDIA is "effectively foreclosed from competing in China's data center computing/compute market" and that the loss of opportunity and the benefit to competitors will have a "material and adverse impact on our business, operating results, and financial condition."

However, the company did NOT provide formal guidance, which limits accountability and makes it harder to assess execution next quarter. The decision to ramp Blackwell and Rubin simultaneously is described as a response to demand, but it also introduces complexity and potential for margin or yield issues that are not quantified.

On capital allocation, the US$80b buyback authorization and the 25× dividend increase are presented as shareholder-friendly but occurred in the same quarter the company issued US$25b of debt, suggesting the cash flow (despite being US$74b in 1H) is not sufficient to fund both growth capex and the new return policy. The company is levering the balance sheet to return capital while the stock trades near all-time highs; that is defensible if the growth continues but increases risk if the cycle turns.

Overall framing: Transparent on the bad news (China, working capital, supply risk), silent on forward guidance, and promotional on capital return. Mixed.

## Positives

- Revenue growth of 106% year-over-year and 18% sequentially is exceptional; NVIDIA is capturing the AI infrastructure buildout.
- Gross margin of 75% is among the highest in semiconductors and improved 260 bps year-over-year despite the scale of shipments, indicating sustained pricing power.
- Operating cash flow of US$74.4b in the first half is massive in absolute terms, even if it lagged net income growth due to working capital timing.
- The company returned US$46.1b to shareholders in six months (US$39.8b buybacks, US$6.3b dividends) and raised the quarterly dividend 25×, signaling confidence.
- Blackwell and Rubin are both shipping, giving NVIDIA a two-generation product overlap that competitors (AMD, Intel) do not have; this sustains the technology lead.
- The US$279b of supply commitments locks in capacity for several years, reducing the risk of a supply shortfall if demand continues.
- Non-GAAP adjustments are absent (no formal non-GAAP EPS), meaning the reported GAAP results are the actual results; SBC is expensed appropriately.

## Negatives / red flags

- NVIDIA is shut out of China's data center compute market (less than 1% of Data Center revenue) and has written off US$4.9b in the past year for unsellable H20 and H200 inventory and purchase obligations; competitors are entrenched and NVIDIA's return to China is unlikely under current US and PRC policies.
- Operating cash flow of US$74.4b covered only 63% of net income (US$118.0b) in 1H FY27 due to a US$24.6b increase in receivables from extended payment terms; this is a timing mismatch, but it means NVIDIA is financing customers and the cash conversion lag could persist for quarters.
- The company issued US$25b of debt in June 2026 despite having US$56.6b of cash and marketable debt securities, because it needed the proceeds to fund US$46.1b of capital return (dividends + buybacks); free cash flow alone was insufficient. This is financial engineering -- levering the balance sheet to return capital while shares trade at elevated multiples.
- Inventory rose US$10.2b in the half and supply commitments jumped from US$119b to US$279b; if demand or product mix shifts (e.g. customers delay Rubin purchases to wait for the next architecture, or a competitor closes the performance gap), NVIDIA will face large write-downs.
- Total equity investment exposure (marketable + non-marketable) is US$90.7b, much of it in early-stage AI companies and AI infrastructure financiers. These are marked to market (for public holdings) or fair-valued quarterly (for private holdings). If the AI investment cycle corrects, NVIDIA will record billions in losses through "Other income, net," creating quarterly earnings volatility unrelated to the core business.
- Gross margin of 75% is at risk from yield issues or competitive pressure. The filing states margin was "approximately flat sequentially as our Blackwell architecture remains the vast majority of our revenue," but the simultaneous Blackwell + Rubin ramp introduces manufacturing complexity (dual supply chains, dual test/packaging flows). Any yield or cost issue will be magnified by the scale of shipments.
- The filing added new risk-factor disclosures on: (i) commitments, guarantees and commercial arrangements (US$108.5b of total guarantees including the US$105b SB Energy / OpenAI PORTS Technology Campus guarantee signed in August 2026, capped but still a massive contingent liability); (ii) AI cloud agreements where NVIDIA commits to cloud capacity that the provider can unilaterally stop providing to NVIDIA and sell to third parties (US$36b of commitments as of Jul 26); (iii) financing arrangements and extended payment terms that affect operating cash flow timing. All three are new, large, and complex; execution risk is high.
- Management did not provide formal guidance for revenue or EPS, making it impossible to hold them accountable to a forecast next quarter; the omission is a negative signal.
- The China regulatory inquiry disclosed on page 19 states that on September 15, 2025, China's antitrust regulators published a preliminary finding that NVIDIA's compliance with US export controls (offering degraded products to the China market) discriminated unfairly against Chinese customers and violated the terms of the Mellanox acquisition approval. If regulators conclude NVIDIA violated Chinese law, the company could face financial penalties, restrictions on its networking business, or other orders. The risk is open-ended and unquantifiable.

## Bottom line

**Bull case:** NVIDIA is the sole supplier of the AI compute infrastructure that every hyperscaler, AI cloud, and enterprise is building. Blackwell and Rubin are both shipping, and the US$279b of locked-in supply commitments (nearly 3× the annual revenue run rate) guarantee the company can meet demand for the next several years. Gross margin of 75% is structurally defensible because no competitor (AMD, Intel, Chinese GPU makers) has the full-stack integration of hardware, software (CUDA, NIM, etc.) and ecosystem. The US$46b returned to shareholders in 1H FY27 is a rounding error relative to the US$229b of equity and the US$118b of net income; the company can afford to lever the balance sheet and still compound at high rates. The China loss is a sunk cost; the rest of the world is growing fast enough to offset it. If the AI infrastructure buildout continues for another 2-3 years, NVIDIA will compound earnings at 50%+ and the current valuation (not disclosed here but implied by the market cap vs the run rate) is reasonable.

**Bear case:** NVIDIA's revenue is 92% Data Center, and Data Center revenue is concentrated among a handful of hyperscalers and AI clouds whose capex plans can change quarter to quarter. The US$24.6b receivables increase and the US$36b of AI cloud agreements where the provider can unilaterally stop providing capacity to NVIDIA both signal that NVIDIA is financing and de-risking its customers' buildouts, not the other way around. The US$90.7b equity portfolio is a venture capital book masquerading as semiconductor earnings; if AI startups and infrastructure financiers cannot monetize the compute they are buying, that portfolio will implode and take billions out of "Other income" each quarter. The US$279b of supply commitments lock NVIDIA into buying components and capacity at today's prices; if the cycle turns, those become write-offs. The US$105b PORTS guarantee for OpenAI's Ohio data center is a bet-the-company contingent liability dressed up as an ecosystem partnership. The simultaneous Blackwell and Rubin ramp is a manufacturing stretch that will pressure yields and margins. The stock is priced for perfection; any demand slowdown, any yield issue, any margin miss will cause a re-rating. China is lost, and France/EU may be next if regulators decide to restrict NVIDIA on competition grounds. The absence of guidance is management buying optionality to lower the bar.

**What would change my view:**
- (Bull) Management reinstates formal quarterly guidance and beats it for three consecutive quarters; gross margin holds above 74% even as Rubin scales; operating cash flow converges back to net income within two quarters (receivables stop growing, implying customers are paying on schedule); equity portfolio mark-to-market swings are <5% of quarterly net income. If all four occur, the growth story is real and sustainable.
- (Bear) Q3 or Q4 FY27 revenue growth decelerates to +10% q/q or less (implying demand saturation); gross margin falls below 72% (yield or competitive pressure); operating cash flow is <75% of net income for a second consecutive quarter (working capital deteriorates further); or the company takes a >US$5b equity portfolio impairment (AI bubble pops). Any one of these four is a red flag; two or more and the thesis is broken.

Current assessment: The metrics are extraordinary (106% revenue growth, 75% gross margin, US$74b operating cash flow in a half). The risks are also extraordinary (US$108.5b of guarantees, US$90.7b equity portfolio, China locked out, no guidance, cash conversion lag). At this scale and this valuation, there is no room for error. The next two quarters will show whether the supply commitments and customer financing arrangements are bridging a temporary mismatch or papering over a demand peak. Hold if you own it, but watch the working capital and the gross margin like a hawk. If receivables are still climbing in Q3 FY27 or gross margin dips below 74%, sell."

## Segments

The business description states two operating segments:

1. **Sleep and Breathing Health**: Devices (CPAP, APAP, bilevel, ASV, ventilators, life support), masks, diagnostic products (ApneaLink Air, NightOwl), accessories, and connected digital health solutions (AirView, myAir). Stated to represent ~51–52% of revenue from devices and ~35–37% from masks/diagnostics/accessories across FY24–FY26, but no actual FY26 segment revenue or margin tables are provided.
2. **Residential Care Software**: Cloud-based SaaS platforms (Brightree for DME/HME, MatrixCare for senior living/skilled nursing/home health/hospice, MEDIFOX DAN in Germany). Stated to represent ~12% of revenue in each of FY24–FY26. On June 30, 2026, ResMed entered a definitive agreement to sell the MatrixCare business for US$490m (subject to adjustments), expected to close Q1 FY27. No income statement, no operating cash flow vs. net income comparison, no working capital movements, no receivables DSO, no inventory turns, no breakdown of cash vs. non-cash charges (SBC, D&A, restructuring), and no disclosure of one-offs or capitalized costs. The accounting policies describe revenue recognition, contract assets (unbilled receivables US$48.7m current, US$14.1m non-current as of Jun 30, 2026 vs. US$51.2m / US$14.6m Jun 30, 2025), and contract liabilities (deferred revenue US$162.9m current, US$171.0m non-current Jun 30, 2026 vs. US$166.0m / US$156.8m Jun 30, 2025), but no context on how revenue, profit, and cash flow evolved during FY26.

## Balance sheet

No consolidated balance sheet is provided. The only balance sheet items mentioned:

- **Total debt**: US$660m as of June 30, 2026 (noted in risk factors; no breakdown of term structure, fixed vs. floating, maturities, or leverage ratio).
- **Contract assets and liabilities**: See Quality of Earnings above. Net contract liability position declined slightly (deferred revenue increased by US$11m net), suggesting modest unwinding of advance billings, but no revenue or cash context.

## Guidance and outlook

No forward guidance, no earnings call commentary, no management outlook section. The business strategy and risk factors provide qualitative context:

- **MatrixCare divestiture**: Expected to close Q1 FY27 for US$490m cash (subject to adjustments). Proceeds likely to reduce net debt or fund buybacks; impact on FY27 revenue and EPS not quantified.
- **Acquisitions**: June 2026 acquisition of Noctrix (restless legs syndrome device, FDA De Novo cleared) expands clinical sleep portfolio; no purchase price or revenue contribution disclosed. FY25 acquisition of VirtuOx (IDTF for home sleep testing) also noted; no FY26 contribution detail.
- **Tariffs and macro risks**: Extensive discussion of potential tariff impacts (U.S. tariffs on imports, retaliatory tariffs, rare earth magnet export controls from China), supply chain disruptions, and inflation. Management states current tariff relief continues (April 2025 CBP notice) but warns that new or increased tariffs, reciprocal tariffs, or trade restrictions could materially increase costs or disrupt supply. No quantification of tariff exposure or mitigation actions.
- **GLP-1 drugs**: Risk factor notes that injectable GLP-1 weight loss drugs (approved for OSA treatment in patients with obesity and moderate-to-severe OSA) may reduce OSA severity if significant weight loss is maintained, potentially reducing demand for PAP devices. Oral GLP-1s under development. No estimate of market impact or timeline.
- **Philips recall overhang**: Risk factor states that Philips continues to operate in the U.S. under a consent decree following its product recall; timing and nature of Philips' substantial return to market uncertain. The recall created temporary demand surge for ResMed devices; Philips' re-entry could reduce ResMed's market share or pricing power.
- **Regulatory**: No change to FDA CPAP coverage or competitive bidding noted for FY26. CMS finalized a National Coverage Determination (NCD) for non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) for COPD effective June 9, 2025, establishing uniform criteria but also specific clinical and documentation requirements; impact on bilevel/HMV sales not quantified. Medicare Sequestration (2% payment reduction) remains in effect; PFS conversion factor reduced 2.93% for CY 2025 but partially offset by 2.5% statutory increase for CY 2026 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (July 2025). VA proposed rule to lower disability ratings for sleep apnea (30% → 10% for CPAP users) not yet finalized; potential demand headwind if enacted.
- **AI and digital health**: Strategy emphasizes AI-powered digital health ecosystem (myAir with Smart Comfort AI-enabled comfort settings, AirView remote monitoring, over 12m myAir users, 35m+ cloud-connected devices). Regulatory landscape for AI evolving; FDA issued SaMD and CDS guidance, Colorado AI Act effective Feb 2026, EU AI Act effective Aug 2024. Compliance costs and product modification risks noted but not quantified.

No FY27 revenue, EPS, or cash flow guidance is provided. No commentary on organic growth rates, pricing trends, or margin outlook.

## Capital allocation

No cash flow statement, no disclosure of dividends declared or paid in FY26, no buyback authorization or execution detail, no M&A spend beyond the Noctrix and MatrixCare transactions (acquisition price for Noctrix not stated; MatrixCare sale price US$490m). Risk factors note that leverage and debt service obligations could limit flexibility; total debt US$660m as of Jun 30, 2026, but no maturity profile, interest expense, or leverage covenant detail. No disclosure of dividend policy, payout ratio, or commitment to return capital.

## Management framing

**Incomplete / Not assessable**: The supplied documents contain no management discussion, no earnings release, no CEO or CFO commentary, and no 8-K exhibit. The 10-K structure includes extensive risk factors (25 pages), business description (24 pages), and accounting policies (detailed revenue recognition, HIPAA, GDPR, AI, fraud & abuse, manufacturing, IP, M&A), but the actual results, variance analysis, and forward-looking statements that would normally appear in Item 7 (MD&A) and Item 8 (financials with footnotes) are missing. This suggests either a partial extraction error (pypdf truncation) or an incomplete filing upload. The auditor consent (KPMG, dated August 13, 2026) references "consolidated financial statements and financial statement schedule II" and "effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting," confirming that a full audit was completed, but those statements are not present in the documents provided. The cover page indicates a Large Accelerated Filer, ICFR attestation = true, no restatement, no shell company—all consistent with a standard 10-K filing—but without the financials and MD&A, no assessment of management transparency, promotional tone, or disclosure quality is possible.

## Positives

- **Market leadership in sleep apnea**: ResMed describes itself as a global leader in digital health and cloud-connected medical devices for sleep-disordered breathing, with over 35 million cloud-connected devices and 12 million myAir users. Extensive installed base and network effects support recurring revenue (masks, accessories, SaaS subscriptions).
- **Portfolio optimization**: Divestiture of MatrixCare (US$490m proceeds expected Q1 FY27) sharpens focus on core sleep, breathing, and connected home healthcare, potentially improving capital efficiency and reducing complexity.
- **Adjacent growth**: Noctrix acquisition (restless legs syndrome) and VirtuOx (IDTF) expand addressable market and vertical integration (diagnostics → devices → software → patient engagement).
- **Digital health moat**: AI-enabled myAir Smart Comfort (FDA-cleared personalized comfort settings), AirView remote monitoring, and integrated SaaS platforms (Brightree, MEDIFOX DAN) create switching costs and data network effects. Over 180 million individual patient accounts supported by Residential Care Software platforms.
- **Regulatory tailwinds**: CMS NCD for NIPPV/COPD (June 2025) establishes uniform national coverage, reducing reimbursement uncertainty for bilevel and HMV products. Medicare telehealth flexibilities extended through Dec 2027, supporting remote patient monitoring.
- **Strong IP position**: ~10,000 pending, allowed, or granted patents and designs globally; ongoing litigation to defend IP suggests active enforcement and barrier to entry.

## Negatives / red flags

- **Incomplete disclosure**: The most significant red flag is that the supplied documents do not include the consolidated financial statements, MD&A, or earnings release. Investors cannot verify revenue, margins, earnings, cash flow, or balance sheet without the full 10-K. This raises the question of whether the filing is complete or whether the extraction process failed.
- **Tariff and supply chain exposure**: Extensive risk factor disclosure on tariffs (U.S. reciprocal tariffs, rare earth magnet export controls from China, retaliatory tariffs), supply chain disruptions (shipping, semiconductor, magnet shortages), and inflation. Management flags material potential impact but provides no quantification of tariff cost exposure, mitigation actions, or margin sensitivity. Singapore and Australia manufacturing sites noted as vulnerable to natural disasters and climate risk.
- **GLP-1 drug threat**: Injectable GLP-1 weight loss drugs approved for OSA treatment in obese patients; oral GLP-1s in development. If sustained weight loss reduces OSA severity, demand for PAP devices could decline. No estimate of market impact, patient overlap, or timeline provided.
- **Philips re-entry risk**: Philips recall (consent decree) created temporary demand surge for ResMed; Philips' eventual return to full market participation could pressure ResMed pricing and market share. Timing and scale uncertain.
- **VA disability rating proposal**: If VA finalizes proposed rule to lower disability ratings for CPAP users (30% → 10%), fewer veterans may seek PAP treatment or more may claim ineffective treatment to maintain higher rating. Veterans represent a meaningful portion of U.S. PAP demand; impact not quantified.
- **Leverage**: US$660m total debt as of Jun 30, 2026; no detail on maturity, interest rate, or covenants. Risk factors note that leverage could limit flexibility, increase vulnerability to economic downturns, and constrain M&A or R&D spending. Cash and net debt position unknown.
- **HIPAA and fraud & abuse compliance**: VirtuOx (IDTF) and Noctrix (DME supplier) subject to direct HIPAA covered entity obligations, Medicare enrollment requirements, Anti-Kickback Statute, Stark Law, False Claims Act, and Civil Monetary Penalties Law. VirtuOx entered US$3m civil settlement and 5-year Corporate Integrity Agreement (CIA) in May 2022 for False Claims Act allegations (incorrect place of service coding, duplicate billing); CIA runs through 2027. Breach of CIA could result in monetary penalties and Medicare exclusion. Noctrix has no Medicare national or local coverage determination for restless legs syndrome device; claims could be denied, requiring refunds. Compliance costs and audit/investigation risk elevated.
- **AI regulatory uncertainty**: FDA, FTC, state laws (Colorado AI Act, CCPA/CPRA biometrics), EU AI Act, and evolving international AI frameworks create compliance complexity and potential product modification or delay risk. myAir Smart Comfort is FDA-cleared AI-enabled SaMD; unclear whether additional AI features in development will face premarket review, clinical trial requirements, or post-market surveillance obligations.
- **Revenue concentration by channel, not customer**: Risk factors state "no single customer accounted for 10% or more of total revenues," but sales are highly concentrated through HME providers, sleep clinics, and health systems. Consolidation among HME providers (noted as ongoing) increases buyer power and pricing pressure. Reimbursement cuts to HME providers flow through to manufacturer pricing and receivables risk.
- **SBC and restructuring**: Accounting policies describe SBC as potential non-GAAP adjustment; risk factors note FY24 included US$34m of intangible impairments related to restructuring. No disclosure of FY26 restructuring charges, SBC expense, or non-GAAP adjustments, so cannot assess whether earnings quality is clean or aggressive.
- **MatrixCare sale pending**: US$490m cash expected Q1 FY27, but transaction subject to closing adjustments and conditions. If deal fails to close or price is reduced, capital allocation and FY27 guidance could be impacted. Transition service agreements and separation costs not detailed.

## Bottom line

**Cannot be determined from the supplied documents.** The materials provided are a partial 10-K filing—cover page, subsidiary list, auditor consent, accounting policies, risk factors, and business description—but no consolidated income statement, balance sheet, cash flow statement, MD&A, or earnings release.
